chocolate-milk-nesquik-made-with-non-dai.title: Nesquik Chocolate Milk made with non-dairy milk

content.title: About
content.content: Nesquik chocolate milk prepared with non-dairy milk combines the sweet cocoa flavor with the convenience of a lactose‑free beverage. Suitable for vegans and people with lactose intolerance.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nesquik was first launched in 1948 as a chocolate powder for milk.
The non‑dairy version was introduced in response to growing demand for plant‑based alternatives.
The ready‑to‑drink product typically contains about 10 g of sugar per 100 ml.
Nesquik powder contains cocoa, sugar and vitamins, but is gluten‑free.
The brand is known for its bright packaging featuring a smiling bunny.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Fortified plant milk provides calcium that supports bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The product often includes riboflavin (B2) and vitamin B12, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from cocoa
items.content: Cocoa supplies flavonoids that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lactose‑free
items.content: Suitable for those with lactose intolerance and for vegan diets.

items.title: Convenient preparation
items.content: Just stir the powder into cold or warm plant milk.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular consumption can contribute to weight gain and elevated blood glucose.

items.title: Soy allergy risk
items.content: If the plant milk base is soy, it may trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Added additives
items.content: The product may contain artificial flavors and preservatives that some people prefer to avoid.

items.title: Not a complete milk substitute
items.content: Although fortified, it does not provide all nutrients found in cow's milk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 2–3 tablespoons of powder with 250 ml of cold or warm plant milk, stir well. It can also be added to smoothies, oatmeal, or used in baking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the powder in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed container. After opening, use within 3–6 months. Keep the plant milk according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned ham is cooked or smoked pork meat packed in a sealed can and heat‑treated for long‑term storage. It is ready to eat straight from the can and is commonly used in salads, sandwiches, and hot dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canned ham is popular in regions with limited access to fresh meat.
Cans are typically sterilized at 121 °C for 30‑45 minutes.
The product may contain additives such as salt, nitrites, flavorings, and sometimes sugar.
There is a “ham in its own juice” version that uses minimal added liquid.
Canned ham is often included in military rations because of its long shelf life.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Ham provides about 15‑18 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: Contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Good source of B1, B3 and B12 vitamins that aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Convenient and long‑lasting
items.content: Sealed cans allow storage for 3‑5 years without refrigeration.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Canned ham often contains 2‑3 g of salt per 100 g, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Nitrites and preservatives
items.content: Nitrites used to preserve color can form potentially harmful compounds when overheated.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pork proteins.

items.title: Saturated fat content
items.content: Ham contains saturated fats, so intake should be limited in cardiovascular disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Ham can be eaten straight from the can, sliced into salads, added to pasta, omelets or hot sandwiches. If desired, briefly warm it in a pan, but avoid high heat to prevent nitrosamine formation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep unopened cans in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, refrigerate and consume within 5‑7 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Rice noodles are thin strands made from rice flour, typically gluten‑free. When cooked they become soft, slightly chewy and translucent. They are a staple in many Asian cuisines, especially Thai, Vietnamese and Chinese dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice noodles originated in Southeast Asia, where rice is the dominant crop.
Unlike wheat noodles, they contain virtually no gluten, making them popular among people with celiac disease.
Various shapes exist: wide (similar to fettuccine), thin (vermicelli) and round (spaghetti‑like).
To speed up preparation, the noodles are often pre‑dried and sometimes lightly toasted.
In Japan a similar product made from rice flour is called "soba" (without eggs).

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rice noodles contain almost no fat, which makes them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Rich source of carbohydrates
items.content: They provide complex carbs that release energy slowly.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Ideal for individuals with gluten intolerance or celiac disease.

items.title: Contains small amounts of B‑vitamins
items.content: Especially thiamine (B1) and niacin (B3), important for metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture after cooking is gentle on the stomach.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice noodles can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Low in protein and fiber
items.content: Compared with whole‑grain alternatives, they provide limited protein and dietary fiber.

items.title: Sodium in ready‑made dishes
items.content: When paired with pre‑made sauces, the dish can become high in sodium.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil the noodles in water for 3‑5 minutes until tender, then rinse with cold water to stop cooking. Add them to soups, stir‑fries, salads, or use as a base for cold Asian dishes with a flavorful sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry rice noodles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked noodles should be eaten within 2‑3 days and stored in the refrigerator in a sealed container.

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken tamale is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a corn‑maize dough (masa) filled with seasoned chicken, spices and sometimes vegetables. The dough is steamed in a banana leaf or corn husk, giving it a moist, fragrant texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tamales are among the oldest foods in the Americas, dating back to the Maya and Aztec civilizations.
They are traditionally prepared in large batches for celebrations such as Day of the Dead and Christmas.
More than 100 regional variations exist, differing in fillings, shapes and cooking methods.
The dough is made from nixtamalized corn flour, which gives tamales their distinctive flavor and texture.
In some regions the filling may include pork, beef, cheese or sweet ingredients in addition to chicken.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The chicken filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Tamales contain niacin, vitamin B6 and folate, which support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The corn masa adds fiber that aids healthy digestion.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Traditional tamales are not sweetened, making them suitable for moderate consumption.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Both chicken and corn contribute iron, important for blood formation.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to corn products, which can cause reactions ranging from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Fillings often contain salt and soy sauce, so people on low‑sodium diets should monitor intake.

items.title: Bacterial growth risk
items.content: Tamales must be cooked thoroughly and cooled quickly; otherwise harmful bacteria can proliferate.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: Because of the masa and meat filling, a serving can be calorie‑rich, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tamales are usually served hot, after removing the banana leaf or corn husk. They can be enjoyed on their own or with salsa, guacamole and sour cream.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked tamales in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze them; reheat by steaming or microwaving before serving.
